strengths: Training-free video reasoning segmentation is a meaningful and timely problem setting, and the proposed DecAF framework (contrastive object-background fusion, complementary video-frame fusion, and attention-consistency-scored SAM2 prompting) is a sensible and well-motivated pipeline that requires no retraining.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5VL) across five referring/reasoning VOS benchmarks, with consistent gains over prior training-free methods (Loc-Head, TAM) and competitive results against several training-based methods (VISA, VideoLISA, GLUS, Veason-R1).

Thorough ablation studies covering each fusion component, rollout variants (V-Max normalization), starting LLM layer, SAM prompting thresholds, consistency-score design, and model scaling — providing good evidence that each design choice contributes.

Honest and detailed analysis: explicit failure cases in the appendix, transparent reporting of reproduction issues with Loc-Head (dataset/model-specific heuristics, sensitivity), and shared prompt templates across all models and datasets, which supports the generalizability claim.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is largely a composition of known techniques (attention rollout, prompt contrast subtraction, frame/video averaging, thresholding, NMS, SAM2 prompting) with many hand-tuned heuristics (middle-layer rollout, fixed τpq=τtrk=0.8, per-frame vs. global normalization), rather than a new technical insight; the components are somewhat ad hoc.

Overclaiming relative to training-based methods: the 'comparable to training-based' claim relies mainly on the best single configuration (Qwen2.5VL-7B); with other MLLMs DecAF lags substantially behind modern training-based SOTA (e.g., 50.3 vs. Veason-R1's 61.3 J&F on ReVOS Overall), and Loc-Head with InternVL3-8B actually beats DecAF on Ref-DAVIS (65.2 vs 61.7).

No computational cost analysis: the pipeline requires multiple MLLM forward passes per video (object, background, category-choice prompts; video plus per-frame modalities) plus many SAM2 tracklet propagations, which could significantly offset the 'training-free' advantage; runtime/compute comparisons against baselines are missing.

Inconsistent terminology ('Decomposed' vs. 'Decoupled' Attention Fusion in Sec. 3.1 and the conclusion), an incomplete code link in the abstract, and some fragile design choices (e.g., dependence on correct object-category prediction for background prompts, sensitivity of thresholding combinations across datasets).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL, Qwen2.5VL) and five benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReasonVOS, ReVOS), which is unusually broad for a training-free segmentation paper

Extensive ablation studies (Tab. 4-8) covering each proposed component (contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale scheme, rollout variants, layer choice, thresholds, consistency scoring), giving reasonable support for the design choices
The paper provides candid discussion of failure modes (Appendix D, Fig. 10) and detailed reproduction notes for baselines (Appendix C), which is commendable transparency

The training-free framing is practically relevant: achieving results comparable to some training-based methods (e.g., within 0.2 of Veason-R1 on ReasonVOS) without any MLLM fine-tuning is a useful demonstration that MLLMs possess intrinsic localization ability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contributions reduce to relatively simple heuristics — subtracting a background attention map from an object attention map, averaging video- and frame-level maps, and thresholding for SAM2 prompts. These are engineering-level refinements of attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020) rather than a principled new mechanism, and no theoretical justification is given for why subtraction or mean-based thresholding is optimal

Heavy reliance on hand-crafted prompt engineering and magic numbers: multiple carefully worded prompt templates, Gaussian smoothing, τpq = 0.8, τtrk = 0.8, middle-layer rollout selection, NMS IoU threshold of 0.7, etc. While ablations show some robustness to thresholds, the overall pipeline's sensitivity to prompt wording (the paper's own critique of TAM rests on tokenization sensitivity) is not analyzed for DecAF itself — how stable are results to rephrasing the object-focused/background prompts?

Claims of 'performance comparable to training-based methods' are overstated: this holds only with the strongest MLLM (Qwen2.5VL-7B) and only on a subset of benchmarks; on MeViS (43.5 vs. 51.3 for GLUS) and ReVOS (50.3 vs. 61.3 for Veason-R1) the gap remains substantial. The abstract-level claim should be tempered

No computational cost analysis: the method requires multiple MLLM forward passes per video (video-level + per-frame image-level + object/background/choice prompts) plus SAM2 propagation of many candidate tracklets. Given the training-free claim is partly a efficiency argument, the inference cost relative to training-based one-pass methods should be reported

Concerning baseline reproductions: the authors report that Loc-Head's reproduced performance dropped drastically from the original paper's numbers (e.g., 74.2 → 34.4 on RefCOCO), and then apply their own SAM prompting to Loc-Head for all comparisons. While well-intentioned, this makes the headline 'outperforms prior training-free methods' comparisons partly against modified baselines; verification of the original protocol is needed

Writing and presentation issues: inconsistent naming ('Decomposed' vs. 'Decoupled' Attention Fusion appears in Sec. 3.1 and the conclusion), a truncated code availability sentence in the abstract, and duplicated/malformed references (Qwen2-VL cited twice; 'Vaswani et al. 2017' attributed oddly). These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread

The absolute quality of attention-only masks is very low (Tab. 1, ~14-25 J&F), and the pipeline's usable performance is almost entirely attributable to SAM2; the paper would benefit from an analysis isolating how much the MLLM attention actually contributes versus what a generic SAM2 automatic-mask-generation baseline with the same number of points would achieve

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically relevant question: whether MLLMs possess intrinsic localization ability that can be exploited training-free for video reasoning segmentation, avoiding model-specific finetuning of LoRA adapters and mask decoders.

The proposed DecAF framework is well-motivated: contrastive object-background fusion directly targets the visual attention sink phenomenon, and complementary video-frame fusion is a sensible multi-scale design that exploits the complementary granularity of video- and frame-level attention.

Comprehensive evaluation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5-VL) and five benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, ReVOS, ReasonVOS), covering both referring and reasoning settings.

The best configuration (Qwen2.5VL-7B) achieves performance comparable to or better than several training-based methods (e.g., surpassing VISA/VideoLISA on Ref-DAVIS, only 0.2 below Veason-R1 on ReasonVOS), which is a notable result for a training-free approach.
Thorough ablations covering each component (contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale scheme, rollout variant, layer choice, thresholds, consistency scoring) and model scale (2B–14B).

Honest and informative appendix: reproduction analysis of TAM and Loc-Head failure modes, disclosed prompt templates applied uniformly across models/datasets, and explicit failure-case analysis rather than only cherry-picked successes.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core ingredients (attention rollout, contrastive/attention-difference maps, SAM prompting, attention-consistency filtering) largely build on existing techniques (Abnar & Zuidema 2020; Lin et al. 2024; VL-SAM), with the main contribution being their adaptation to video reasoning segmentation rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The pipeline is heuristic-heavy: many hand-designed components (Gaussian smoothing, min-max normalization, Otsu/mean thresholding, NMS with IoU 0.7, fixed τpq/τtrk=0.8, the s^ac definition) accumulated without a unifying principle; robustness claims rest on grid searches rather than principled justification.

The method depends on the MLLM correctly identifying the object category via a single-word QA prompt; the paper does not report how often this category identification fails and how such failures propagate (a natural ablation is missing), which is a single point of failure for reasoning-heavy queries.

Comparisons to training-free baselines are limited essentially to Loc-Head and TAM; there may be other training-free grounding/segmentation pipelines (e.g., VL-SAM adapted to video, or detector+SAM2 combinations) that are not compared.

Some experimental presentation raises questions: Table 2 shows LLaVA-7B vs. LLaVA-OV-7B for Loc-Head vs. DecAF (not identical MLLMs), and Qwen2.5VL-based results dominate headline claims, so part of the gain over training-based methods may come from the stronger underlying MLLM rather than DecAF itself.

Minor inconsistencies and typos: 'Decoupled' vs. 'Decomposed' Attention Fusion in Sec. 3.1 vs. elsewhere, incomplete code URL in the abstract, 'rank and tracklet candidates' phrasing, and the main text claims qualitative results are in the appendix while figures are sparsely labeled (some qualitative rows appear visually similar across rows in Figs. 5–9).

strengths: Strong empirical results for a training-free approach: DecAF consistently outperforms training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) across three MLLM families and five datasets, and even surpasses training-based methods (including Veason-R1, which RL-trains the same MLLM) on ReasonVOS, supporting the central claim that MLLM reasoning translates to localization ability.

Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: extensive ablations covering each fusion component, rollout normalization, layer choice, thresholds, scoring design, and model scalability (Tabs. 4-8), plus a prompt-robustness analysis (Tabs. 10-12) showing the method is not overfit to specific prompt formulations.

Careful and honest baseline treatment: the appendix transparently documents reproduction difficulties with Loc-Head and TAM (e.g., head-selection heuristics not generalizing, tokenization sensitivity), and provides a naive native-grounding baseline (Tab. 9) that fairly isolates the contribution of attention-based grounding over Qwen2.5-VL's built-in grounding.
Includes qualitative results, failure case analysis, and discussion of limitations (small/thin objects, part-level ambiguity), which strengthens credibility.

The problem framing (training-free video reasoning segmentation via attention rollout) is timely and the proposed contrastive object-background subtraction and video-frame complementary fusion are intuitively well-motivated and validated by ablations (e.g., 12.4→20.7 on Ref-DAVIS attention masks).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a composition of well-known components — attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020), contrastive prompt subtraction, multi-scale averaging, Otsu/NMS heuristics, and SAM2 point prompting. Each individual mechanism is simple, and the contribution rests more on engineering than on a new technical insight.

Heavy reliance on hand-crafted heuristics: the pipeline involves multiple thresholds (τpq, τtrk), Gaussian smoothing, min-max normalization choices, tracklet scoring, and carefully designed prompt templates. While robustness is studied, the system's dependence on such design choices weakens the claim of a principled, generalizable framework.

The attention maps alone remain weak (Tab. 1: ~20-25 J&F), far below even modest segmentation quality; the headline results depend critically on SAM2. The paper is candid about this, but it means the core localization signal is only a coarse prompt, and the practical value of the pure attention-mask path is limited.

Computational cost is unaddressed: the pipeline runs the MLLM multiple times per video (video-level, frame-level, object and background prompts, category choice), which may be substantially more expensive than training-based inference. A training-free method with hidden heavy inference cost should report runtime/FLOPs comparisons.

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: Loc-Head is re-implemented with the authors' own SAM prompting scheme rather than its original prompting (partly justified by reproduction failure), and some reported Loc-Head numbers differ noticeably from its paper; potential contamination of base MLLM training data on these public VOS benchmarks is not discussed.

Gains are concentrated on Qwen2.5VL-7B (e.g., 75.2 on Ref-DAVIS), while on other backbones (InternVL3, LLaVA-OV) results are less dominant and sometimes below baselines (e.g., Loc-Head beats DecAF on Ref-DAVIS with InternVL3-8B in Tab. 2), suggesting the approach benefits disproportionately from strong native grounding/resolution capabilities of one model family.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) across five VOS benchmarks, with both attention-only masks and SAM2-prompted dense masks.

The ablation studies (Tables 4-8) are thorough, covering each fusion component, rollout variants, layer selection, thresholds, and the attention consistency score, so the contribution of each design choice is reasonably supported.

The paper is transparent about limitations: it admits coarse attention maps, low contour accuracy, and provides genuine failure case analyses (Fig. 9) and part-level/non-explicit expression analyses in the appendix.

The prompt robustness analysis (Appendix F) and the native-grounding baseline (Table 9) strengthen the case that the method is not merely exploiting prompt tuning, and address an obvious alternative baseline (Qwen2.5-VL + SAM2).
Code availability is claimed, and a training-free pipeline is practically interesting for the community.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The method is an ensemble of known techniques: attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020), contrastive/subtractive attention prompting, multi-scale video-frame fusion, Otsu thresholding, NMS, and point prompting of SAM2. Each component is a heuristic patch rather than a principled advance, and the paper offers little theoretical insight into why MLLM attention should support segmentation.

The framing of 'reasoning segmentation as video QA' is thinner than claimed: the pipeline actually reduces the expression to a single object category ('respond with a single word'), and the localization is driven by that category identification. This weakens the claim that complex reasoning is directly translated into localization, and the mechanism connecting reasoning to spatial grounding remains unexamined (no analysis of which tokens/layers actually carry grounding signals beyond a coarse layer ablation).

Comparison fairness with training-based methods (Tables 2 and 3) is questionable. Methods like VISA, VideoLISA, and VRS-HQ are built on substantially older/weaker MLLMs (ChatUniVi, LLaVA-Phi-3); attributing DecAF's gains over them to the training-free design conflates backbone improvements with method contributions. Only Veason-R1 shares the same MLLM, and the claim of 'surpassing all training-based methods on ReasonVOS' rests on a single benchmark with a small test set (458 samples).

No inference cost analysis. The pipeline requires multiple MLLM forward passes (object video, background video, per-frame object, background, and category choice prompts), plus SAM2 propagation with NMS and tracklet scoring. Training-free does not mean cheap; efficiency should be reported and compared against single-pass training-based methods.

Sensitivity to empirical hyperparameters is a concern despite the claimed robustness: rollout starting layer, Gaussian smoothing, Otsu vs. mean thresholding (Table 7 shows a 10-point swing), and thresholds τpq/τtrk are all tuned, and no variance or multiple-run statistics are reported anywhere.

Attention rollout is a known unreliable interpretability proxy; the paper motivates its use informally ('a plausible approach') rather than validating that rollout scores reflect the model's actual decision pathway, e.g., via counterfactual or perturbation analysis.

Presentation issues: several typos ('stoped', 'ans SAM masks', 'oname'), notation V appears with different meanings (attention map vs. component), and key details (Gaussian smoothing parameters, number of sampled frames per stage) are deferred to an appendix with an empty 'Code is available at' link, hurting reproducibility in its current form.

strengths: Strong empirical results for a training-free approach: DecAF consistently outperforms the main training-free baseline (Loc-Head) across three MLLM families and five datasets, and achieves comparable or superior performance to training-based methods (e.g., surpassing all training-based methods on ReasonVOS despite Veason-R1 training the same backbone with RL).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: five datasets covering referring and reasoning VOS, multiple MLLM backbones and scales (Tab. 8), and a large set of ablations covering the fusion components (Tab. 4), rollout variants and layer choice (Tab. 5), SAM prompting thresholds (Tab. 6), attention consistency scoring (Tab. 7), and prompt robustness (Tabs. 10-12).

Good scientific hygiene: honest reporting of failure cases (Fig. 9), detailed reproduction analysis of Loc-Head explaining discrepancies and adaptation issues (Appendix C), and an important naive-baseline comparison using Qwen2.5-VL's native grounding (Tab. 9) that strengthens the claim that DecAF's gains are not trivially available from MLLM grounding.

Practical significance: requiring no retraining makes the method model-agnostic and cheap to adopt, and the pipeline naturally supports multi-object localization; the paper clearly articulates why head-selection heuristics (Loc-Head) generalize poorly while rollout-based fusion is more robust.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the individual components — attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020), contrastive background subtraction, video-frame multi-scale fusion, and attention-guided SAM prompting — are each well-established; the contribution is largely a carefully engineered combination and a head-weighting normalization variant, which may be viewed as incremental.

No efficiency/runtime analysis. The pipeline requires multiple MLLM forward passes per video (video-level and frame-level, object and background prompts, plus category-choice queries) and many SAM2 tracklets; the claim of 'training-free' advantage over training-based methods is not complemented by an inference-cost comparison, which is important for practical impact claims.

Potential evaluation leakage concern: hyperparameters (rollout layer index, τpq, τtrk, consistency-score design) are ablated and selected on ReasonVOS, yet the paper frames ReasonVOS results as a zero-shot comparison against training-based methods. The zero-shot claim should be softened or validated on a strictly held-out setting.

The method depends on a fragile intermediate step: collapsing the target to a single object category via prompts may fail for expressions involving attributes, parts, or reasoning beyond a category (the part-level analysis in Appendix I shows SAM2 masks then become unreliable), and there is no quantitative analysis of category-prediction error rates.

Attention-mask-only results are very low in absolute terms (F much lower than J), indicating the attention maps alone are weak; the strong final numbers lean heavily on SAM2, so the specific attribution of gains to DecAF vs. the SAM prompting pipeline could be more clearly dissected.

Several design choices are heuristic (middle-layer rollout start, Gaussian smoothing, subtraction + clamping, averaging-based fusion) without theoretical justification; while ablations show they work, the method reads as a bag of tricks.
